newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Feb 28.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Feb 28.

text.p: Representatives from Australian Consolidated Press, publishers of Metro, have been summoned before the winebox commission this morning to explain several issues arising from an article "Oops, Wrong Winebox" published in the magazine this week. Written by Keith "Slasher" Davies, erstwhile public relations consultant to the Serious Fraud Office, the story discredits the commission, Auckland businessman Stephen Lunn -- the man widely credited with being the winebox whistleblower -- the journalists who broke the winebox story, Winston Peters' lawyer Brian Henry, and witnesses who have, over the past two weeks, given evidence against SFO director Chas Sturt. Page 1.

New Zealand apple growers sponsored an 85,000 pounds British motor racing deal that soured with only seven out of 12 races run, the original promoter out of the pocket, the driver without a car, and the Apple and Pear Board's Enza UK backing away from the wrangle. Auckland businessman Keith Abbott is claiming breach of contract and interference by Enza New Zealand (UK) executives after he was pushed out of the racing car sponsorship deal he brought to the table in 1994. Page 1.

A group of National MPs is making another bid to split from the party's Auckland division. The rift was triggered by a festering row over the chairmanship of divisional head, John Slater. The MPs don't want to be named at this stage, but they are using a sweeping review of the party's structure to state their case for breaking the huge Auckland division into two or three "sub-divisions". The region would be split into north, west, and south. Page 1.

Oysters were merely the first course in the deal struck between the government and the Treaty of Waitangi Fisheries Commission this week. The commission's role in the management of commercial fisheries has been fortified -- the commission must be consulted by the Fisheries Ministry on decisions to bring species within the quota management system (QMS). And the deal advances prospects of 20 percent shares in other species being distributed to Maori. Page 2.

Tough new tax penalties will give the Inland Revenue Department real teeth to go after corporates suspected of exploiting loopholes or playing games with the taxman. The new penalties up the ante for businesses aggressively interpreting the law or engaging in tax efficient transactions. From the April tax year, these businesses can be fined for such "misbehaviour". The new penalty and compliance regime introduces a five-tier sliding scale of fines applied according to how badly the taxpayer is deemed to have behaved. The worse the behaviour, the higher up the scale they end. Page 3.

Reports that Tranz Rail's most powerful shareholder, Wisconsin Central, has the United States' worst railroad safety record has alarmed a local union. A safety audit of Wisconsin Central late last year found the company's accident rate was nearly double all other US railroads, the US Journal of Commerce says. Its accident rate was 72 percent higher than similarly sized carriers. Page 3.

The licensed real estate agents' monopolistic grip on the housing market is weakening. Leading the charge to introduce greater competition into the industry are the nationally-franchised Private Sale Company and West Auckland company Home Search. Both have established niche presences. Both have greater ambitions. Over the years a number of home vendor self-help operations have started up. Most closed down shortly after opening -- some after the Real Estate Institute launched legal proceedings. Home Search and the Private Sale Company say they are here to stay. Current consumer trends appear in their favour. Page 4.

Market speculation that Qantas is trying to sell its 19.4 percent Air NZ stake was fuelled by this week's news that the two airlines had terminated their six-year code-sharing arrangement, saying the trans-Tasman deal is now "commercially inappropriate". The airlines cited new international alignments and the slowing of growth in Asian markets as the main reasons for change. Qantas chairman Gary Pemberton denies the sale of the Air NZ stake is imminent. But The Independent understands the decision to sell has already been made -- only the price and the identity of the buyer have yet to be decided. Page 5.

601 Digital receiver Laurie Chilcott is investigating whether the Auckland-based video production company's assets have been transferred into Schober Enterprises -- a company associated with former Aotearoa Television director Derek Burns and accountant Peter Brannigan -- a key wine-box inquiry witness. Debenture-holder Reston Griffith appointed the receiver last Friday. Griffith sold 601 Digital late last year to another Burns and Brannigan company, Alroy Enterprises, for $800,000, to be paid over several months. Some of the assets were subsequently on-sold to beleagured Maori television station Aotearoa Television Network at a substantial premium. Page 5.

Hong Kong's Independent Commission Against Corruption begins a two-week sitting in the High Court at Auckland on Monday. The hearing is part of the long running fraud trial against ex-Auckland traffic cop turned immigration consultant Aaron Nattrass. Nattrass denies the 13 fraud and deception charges relating to his work as an immigration consultant in Hong Kong in 1988. The decision to bring the trial to Auckland came after it was learned a crucial prosecution witness was too ill to travel to Hong Kong. Page 7.
